rationale: C12 is the closest because both proclamations concern displaying the United States flag and use a direct operative command that the flag be displayed. But C12 is an annual Flag Day observance limited to June 14, while the child invokes a specific statutory power to modify flag-display rules and creates a perpetual day-and-night exception for Fort McHenry. The shared wording is natural to the subject and does not amount to material drafting machinery. C17 has a superficially similar statute-quotation-to-proclamation structure, and C25 concerns a national monument, but neither supplies distinctive language or operative structure adapted in the child.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the flag of the United States shall hereafter be displayed at Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine at all times during the day and night
shared_material.parent_excerpt: do hereby direct that the flag of the United States be displayed on all Government buildings on June 14, 1948
shared_material.explanation: C12 shares the flag-display formulation, but this is ordinary language dictated by the common subject; the duration, legal authority, purpose, and operative effect materially differ.

shared_material.child_excerpt: Whereas the joint resolution of Congress ... contains the following provisions
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Whereas section 3228(f) of the Internal Revenue Code provides in part as follows
shared_material.explanation: C17 likewise quotes governing statutory text before an operative proclamation, but that generic statutory-recital structure does not establish reusable drafting.

shared_material.child_excerpt: displayed at Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine
shared_material.parent_excerpt: added to and reserved as a part of the Fort Matanzas National Monument
shared_material.explanation: C25 shares a national-monument setting, but its land-reservation, boundary-description, warning, and administrative provisions are absent from the child.
